title: 1 Samuel
subtitle: Prophet, priest and the first kings
lead: 1 Samuel tells how Israel moved from judges to kings. It begins with a childless woman praying at Shiloh and ends with a king dead on a mountain. Between them stand three men: Samuel, the prophet who anoints two kings; Saul, the tall Benjaminite who is chosen and then rejected; and David, the shepherd boy who kills a giant, is hunted for years, and waits for God to give him the throne.

It is one of the great works of storytelling in the ancient world, full of reversals: the barren woman sings, the proud priest falls, the captured ark humbles its captors, and the king the people asked for loses everything to the one God chose. Its themes of power, prayer, loyalty and listening to God have shaped Jewish and Christian ideas of kingship and of the Messiah, the LORD's anointed.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a): Samuel wrote it up to his death, and the prophets Gad and Nathan finished it. Most critical scholars: part of the Deuteronomistic History, edited in the 7th–6th centuries BC from older sources.
Set about 1100–1010 BC, from Samuel's birth to Saul's death. The sources may go back to the 10th century BC; the book reached its present form in the late monarchy or the exile.
The hill country of Ephraim, Benjamin and Judah; the Philistine plain; the wilderness of Judah; and the Jezreel Valley and Mount Gilboa.
Historical narrative with prophetic stories, speeches, lists, and poems (Hannah's song).
Hebrew. The Hebrew text of Samuel is unusually damaged, and the Greek and the Dead Sea scrolls often help.

31 chapters, 810 verses. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book in Hebrew; the Greek calls them 1 and 2 Kingdoms (1–2 Reigns), and the Vulgate and the King James Version subtitle this book "the First Book of the Kings"

audience.to: Israelites who lived well after Saul and David and needed to know how their kingdom began. The book looks back on its events. It explains that a prophet was once called a seer (9:9), and it says that customs and places remain "to this day" (5:5; 6:18; 27:6; 30:25). Who exactly those readers were depends on when the book was put together. The answers run from David's own court, through Judah under King Josiah, to the exiles in Babylon after 586 BC, who had lost both their king and their temple.
audience.why: To explain how Israel came to have kings, and why God's choice passed from Saul to David. The book shows that God raises the low and brings down the proud (2:1–10), that he wants listening more than sacrifice (15:22), and that he looks at the heart (16:7). It also answers a hard question: was David a rebel who stole Saul's throne? Again and again the story shows David refusing to harm "the LORD's anointed" (24:6; 26:9), while Saul destroys himself. Knowing the readers changes the reading. For people living under David's sons, it is a defense of the dynasty. For exiles with no king, it is a warning that kings and people alike fall when they will not listen. It is also a reminder that God can still raise up someone from the dust.
views: Written by the prophets, close to the events

Jewish tradition says Samuel wrote the book up to his death, and the prophets Gad and Nathan finished it (Bavli Bava Batra 15a; compare 1 Chronicles 29:29). On this view the first readers were Israel in the time of David and Solomon, and the book is the prophets' record of how God chose a king.

Many scholars think the core stories, especially the History of David's Rise (16:14 to 2 Samuel 5), were written at David's or Solomon's court. They read it as a royal apology, that is, a work written to defend a king against charges. On this view it answers people in Benjamin and among Saul's supporters who said David was a traitor who served the Philistines and took Saul's throne. Every charge is met: David did not kill Saul, was away from the battle, and was chosen by God.
Part of a history for Josiah's Judah

Frank Moore Cross and others see a first edition of the history from Deuteronomy to Kings written under King Josiah in the late 7th century BC. Samuel then shows readers in Jerusalem why David's line is the true one and why the king must obey God's word through the prophets.
The Deuteronomistic History, written after the fall

The Deuteronomistic History is the long history from Deuteronomy to Kings, written in the language of Deuteronomy. Martin Noth argued that one writer composed it after 586 BC, probably in the land of Judah, to explain why the disaster was just. For its readers, Samuel's warnings about kings (8:11–18; 12:25) had come true. Noth saw no promise of a future in it. Robert Polzin, reading the book as a literary whole, hears 1 Samuel as the exiles' reflection on why kingship failed.
A history that still holds hope

Gerhard von Rad answered Noth that the history holds on to God's promise to David, and ends with the captive king set free (2 Kings 25:27–30). On this view the book kept the memory of God's choice of David alive for a people without a throne.

Literary readers such as Robert Alter and J. P. Fokkelman leave the dates open and read the book as a whole. For them the first readers matter less than the questions the story raises for any reader about power, ambition, loyalty and God's freedom to choose.

A few scholars date the David stories much later. John Van Seters thought they were written after the exile. A. Graeme Auld argued that Samuel–Kings and Chronicles both grew out of one older shared story of the kings.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Samuel, Saul and David lived around 1100–970 BC, and the book records real events, drawing on court records and prophets' writings (1 Chronicles 29:29).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars see older sources woven together (an ark story, a rise-of-David story, pro- and anti-monarchy strands) and edited into the Deuteronomistic History. Some see David's story as royal apology, written to defend a usurper; minimalists doubt much of it.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Readers of every school study the book as narrative art: reversals of fortune (Hannah's song), paired characters (Eli's sons and Samuel, Saul and David), and the narrator's silences about motive.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The Talmud credits Samuel with writing the book up to his death (Bava Batra 14b–15a). Hannah's prayer is the rabbis' model of prayer (Berakhot 31a), and her story is read on Rosh Hashanah.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Hannah's song lies behind Mary's (Luke 1:46–55). David, the anointed shepherd from Bethlehem chosen over his brothers, is read as a type of Christ, the Son of David.

authorship: Traditional view: Samuel, Gad and Nathan

The Talmud says that Samuel wrote his book, and that Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet completed it after his death (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), drawing on 1 Chronicles 29:29, which mentions the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer. Notes such as "to this day" (5:5; 6:18; 27:6) and the explanation of the word "seer" (9:9) show a writer later than the events, which traditional readers attribute to the prophets who finished the work.
Critical scholarship: sources and the Deuteronomistic History

Martin Noth (1943) placed Samuel within a history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, edited in the exile. Within it scholars see older blocks: an ark narrative (4:1–7:1, with 2 Samuel 6), suggested by Leonhard Rost, though Patrick Miller and J. J. M. Roberts argued it began with Eli's sons in chapter 2 and ended at 7:1; stories of Saul's rise; a long History of David's Rise (16:14–2 Samuel 5); and pro- and anti-monarchy strands in chapters 8–12. Many read the David story as a royal apology, written to defend David against charges that he usurped Saul's throne.

Robert Alter, Robert Polzin, J. P. Fokkelman and others read 1 Samuel as a deliberate whole, with paired characters (Eli's sons and Samuel, Saul and David, Michal and Abigail), recurring words such as "ask," "heavy" and "see," and a narrator who often withholds motive. Many find the portraits of Saul and David among the most complex in ancient literature.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level, drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew and then checked verse by verse against other English versions, and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. YHWH is "the LORD." Key terms are kept steady across the whole Bible: YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies" (1:3); hesed is "loyal love"; nagid, when it names the leader God designates, is "ruler," and melekh is "king" (9:16; 10:1); meshiach YHWH is "the LORD's anointed" (2:10); ro'eh is "seer" (9:9), and chozeh, a different word, will be "visionary"; and the Spirit "sweeps down on" (tsalach) Saul and David as on Samson (10:6; 16:13). The word play on kaved, "heavy," and kavod, "glory," is kept where English allows (2:30; 4:18; 4:21; 5:6). Hannah's song (2:1–10) and David's lament (in 2 Samuel 1) are set in poetic lines.

The Hebrew, the Greek and the Dead Sea scrolls

Samuel's Hebrew text has suffered more in copying than almost any other book. The Greek Septuagint was translated from a Hebrew text that was often better, and the scroll 4QSam-a from Qumran Cave 4 (about 50–25 BC) frequently agrees with it. Where the evidence is strong the Plain follows the Greek or the scroll, and says so in the variant: for example the three-year-old bull (1:24), Hannah's own vow (1:23), Eli's blessing (2:20), the longer anointing speech (10:1) and the paragraph about Nahash (10:27). Elsewhere it keeps the Hebrew and shows the other readings beside it.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book falls into three overlapping stories. Chapters 1–7 tell of Samuel and the fall of Eli's house, with the ark's capture and return (4–6) at the center. Chapters 8–15 tell of Saul: the request for a king, his rise, his victories and his rejection. Chapters 16–31 tell of David's rise under Saul's shadow, from his anointing and the duel with Goliath through years as a fugitive to Saul's death on Gilboa. Each part overlaps the next: Samuel anoints Saul, and Saul still rules while David is anointed. Hannah's song (2:1–10), which ends with God's king, sets the theme for the whole.

1 Samuel holds two views of kingship side by side. God calls the request a rejection of himself (8:7; 10:19; 12:12), and Samuel lists what a king will take (8:11–17). Yet the book also makes the case for kings. Judges ended with no king in Israel and everyone doing what was right in his own eyes; God had promised Abraham kings (Genesis 17:6) and given Judah the scepter (Genesis 49:10); Deuteronomy plans for a king; and Hannah's song ends with God's king (2:10). God himself chooses Saul to rescue his people, because he has heard their cry (9:16), and later chooses David, a man to suit his own heart (13:14). Critical scholars have often explained this by separate sources; literary and traditional readers see a deliberate tension: a king is allowed, but only one who listens to God's word through the prophet. That is the test Saul fails (13:13–14; 15:22–23) and the hope that David, despite his sins, comes to carry.

The book's world fits much of what archaeology shows of the eleventh century BC: small villages in the hill country, Philistine cities on the coast with their own pottery and temples, and a destruction at Shiloh. The text describes Philistine control of smiths (13:19–22); archaeologists debate whether the Philistines had any real advantage in iron, since iron is rare on both sides in this period. An inscription from Ekron names the city and its kings; excavations at Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron and Tell es-Safi (Gath) show the Philistine cities' culture, while Gaza lies under the modern city and is barely dug. The Tel Dan inscription (9th century BC) names the "house of David." Historians differ on how large Saul's kingdom and David's early following were, and on how much of the detailed storytelling preserves real memory. Traditional readers take the account as reliable history from close to the time; minimalist scholars doubt most of it; many fall in between.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read 1 Samuel
sections.b: In Jewish tradition Samuel is counted among the Former Prophets. Hannah's prayer taught the rabbis how to pray, and her story and song are read on Rosh Hashanah. The rabbis debated whether asking for a king was a sin (Bavli Sanhedrin 20b), and honored David as the ancestor of the Messiah. For Christians, Hannah's song lies behind Mary's (Luke 1:46–55), Samuel's childhood behind Luke's account of Jesus' (Luke 2:52), and David, the anointed shepherd from Bethlehem, is a type of Christ, the Son of David. Both traditions have drawn political teaching from chapter 8 and moral lessons from Saul's fall.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book about asking and listening
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: 1 Samuel turns on two verbs. One is sha'al, "ask": Hannah asks for a son and gives him back (1:20, 1:27–28); the people ask for a king (8:10; 12:13, 12:17); Saul, whose name means "asked for," later asks God and receives no answer (14:37; 28:6). The other is shama', "listen": Samuel says "Your servant is listening" (3:10), the people refuse to listen to Samuel (8:19), and Samuel tells Saul that listening is better than sacrifice (15:22). I suggest the book is built so that the right kind of asking leads to listening, and the wrong kind ends in silence: Saul, the king who was asked for, ends at Endor asking a dead prophet because God no longer answers him. Scholars have long noted both words; the claim that they form the book's backbone is my own suggestion.

The doorway of a small stone sanctuary on a hill at Shiloh, with a lamp burning inside. A woman, Hannah, stands at the doorway praying, lips moving with no sound, tears on her face. Beside the doorpost an old priest, Eli, sits on a seat watching her with a doubtful look. Behind them, people of the festival eat and drink among tents and olive trees.

The standard critical commentary, especially strong on the Hebrew, Greek and Qumran texts.
